42-007.r: Founder of the British Empire in India → Robert Clive; he defeated Nawab Siraj-ud-daula at Plassey on 23 June 1757.

42-008.r: "Heaven-Born General" (William Pitt's phrase) → Robert Clive; Governor of Bengal twice (1758-1760, 1765-1767); made Shuja-ud-daula and Shah Alam II sign the Treaty of Allahabad.

42-009.r: Plassey (Palasi) battlefield → on the Bhagirathi river, Nadia district, West Bengal.

42-010.r: Mir Qasim shifted his capital from Murshidabad to Munger to escape Calcutta's interference; he trained his army on European lines and ran an arms factory at Munger.

42-011.r: Most decisive battle for British supremacy → Buxar, 22/23 Oct 1764: Hector Munro defeated Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-daula and Shah Alam II (then ruler of Delhi).
42-011.t: Plassey began British power; Buxar is called the most decisive battle.

42-016.r: Treaty signed after the Battle of Buxar (1764) → Treaty of Allahabad (1765).

42-017.r: Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa → granted by Mughal emperor Shah Alam II on 12 August 1765, after the Treaty of Allahabad; Clive was Governor.

42-021.r: After the Treaty of Allahabad, Clive made Mohd. Raza Khan Deputy Diwan at Murshidabad; Nazm-ud-daula (son of Mir Jafar) was accepted as Nawab of Bengal.

42-022.r: First hill tribe met after the 1765 Diwani → Khasi (British reached Sylhet in 1765); Khasis later revolted under Tirot Sing.

42-023.r: Raja Tikait Rai → Artha Mantri (diwan) of Nawab Asaf-ud-daula; Hindus often held high posts in Oudh (e.g. Raja Naval Rai under Safdar Jung). Both correct.

42-024.r: Order: Ambur (1749) → Plassey (1757) → Wandiwash (1760) → Buxar (1764). At Wandiwash the British defeated the French under Count Lally.

42-028.r: Correct pair: Battle of Wandiwash → French vs East India Company (1760). Buxar was Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-daula and Shah Alam II vs British under Hector Munro.

42-029.r: Strongest opponents of the British → Marathas; crushed only after three Anglo-Maratha Wars; British lost the first one (ended by Treaty of Salbai).

43-001.r: Ranjit Singh's kingdom included Srinagar (not Delhi or Kabul); he belonged to the Sukerchakia Misl of his father Maha Singh.

43-004.r: Capital of Ranjit Singh → Lahore, seized in 1799 (after he returned Zaman Shah's cannons lost in the Jhelum, 1798).

43-005.r: Adalat-i-Ala (high court hearing appeals from district and provincial courts) → set up by Ranjit Singh at Lahore.

43-006.r: Treaty of Amritsar, 25 April 1809 → Ranjit Singh and Lord Minto I (signed by Charles Metcalfe); Sutlej fixed as the boundary.

43-007.r: Ranjit Singh got the Kohinoor from Shah Shuja, grandson of Ahmad Shah Abdali, who held the Kabul throne from 1803.

43-008.r: "God intended me to look upon all religions with one eye..." → Maharaja Ranjit Singh (born 13 Nov 1780, Gujranwala).
43-008.h: He had lost one eye - the quote turns his one eye into equal respect for all faiths.

43-009.r: Treaty of Lahore (March 1846): Maharaja ceded all territory beyond the Sutlej forever and gave up the forts between Sutlej and Beas → I and II correct.

43-010.r: Successor of Ranjit Singh → Kharak (Khadag) Singh, who took the throne on Ranjit Singh's death in 1839.

43-011.r: Last king of the Sikh empire → Maharaja Duleep Singh (reigned 1843-1849).

43-013.r: Duleep Singh died in Paris, 22 or 23 Oct 1893; became Christian 1853, returned to Sikhism 1886; did visit Russia; cremated in England, not Nasik.

43-014.r: False: Duleep Singh's pension Rs 2,50,000 → it was set at four to five lakh. True: Dalhousie's proclamation of 29 March 1849 merged all Punjab into British India.

43-015.r: Board of Three for Punjab (1849) → Henry Lawrence (President), John Lawrence, Charles Grenville Mansel; not H.M. Elliot or Robert Montgomery (both answers).

43-016.r: First Anglo-Mysore War (1767-69) → Haidar Ali won; took Mangalore 1768, reached Madras 1769; English signed Treaty of Madras (April 1769) on his terms.

43-017.r: Modern armoury at Dindigul, 1755 → Haidar Ali, sent there by the Mysore king to control the rebel Palayams.

43-018.r: Battle of Porto Novo (1781) → Sir Eyre Coote defeated Haidar Ali; earlier Haidar and Tipu beat Colonel Baillie at Pollilur (10 Sept 1780).

43-019.r: Tipu Sultan's capital → Srirangapatna; there he joined the Jacobin Club and planted the 'Tree of Liberty' to mark the France-Mysore alliance.

43-020.r: Indian ruler who set up embassies abroad on modern lines → Tipu Sultan (Iran, Istanbul, Afghanistan, France).

43-021.r: 1780 → Colonel William Baillie's British army defeated at Pollilur (by Tipu and Haidar Ali), after Haidar's siege of Arcot.

43-022.r: Treaty of Srirangapatna (March 1792) → Tipu Sultan and Cornwallis, ended Third Anglo-Mysore War (1790-92); Tipu ceded half his kingdom.

43-023.r: Tipu Sultan died in 1799 defending Srirangapatna in the Fourth (final) Anglo-Mysore War.

43-024.r: Correct: Fourth Anglo-Mysore War → Tipu defeated and killed. First (1767-1769) → Haidar won, Treaty of Madras; Second (1780-1784) → Treaty of Mangalore; Third (1790-92) → Tipu lost territory.

43-025.r: Treaty of Allahabad → 1765; Treaty of Salbai → 1782; Treaty of Mangalore → 1784; Treaty of Madras → 1769.
43-025.h: Order A-M-S-M: Allahabad, Madras, Salbai, Mangalore - the two Mysore treaties bracket Salbai.

43-026.r: Begum Samru built the famous church at Sardhana near Meerut; her husband was the European Walter Reinhardt; she ruled Sardhana after his death.

43-027.r: Wrong: Ali Mardan Khan began Bengal revenue farming → it was Murshid Quli Khan. True: Ranjit Singh's Lahore cannon foundries; Jai Singh's Sanskrit Euclid; Tipu funded Sringeri's Sharda idol.

43-028.r: Only true: Mir Jafar plotted with the English at Plassey (1757). Third Panipat (1761) → Abdali beat Marathas, not Ibrahim Lodi; Tipu died in Fourth Mysore War (1799).

44-001.r: First Governor-General of Bengal → Warren Hastings (Regulating Act 1773), not Clive; first Governor-General of India → William Bentinck (Charter Act 1833). Only statement 2 correct.
44-001.t: Don't confuse GG of Bengal (Hastings, 1773) with GG of India (Bentinck, 1833).

44-004.r: Order: Battle of Buxar (22/23 Oct 1764) → Clive returns (3 May 1765) → Treaty of Allahabad (Aug 1765) → Warren Hastings Governor of Bengal (1772).
44-004.c: Answer not printed; explanation gives 3, 1, 2, 4 = option (b); also notes Hastings was Governor of Bengal, not India.

44-005.r: Not true: Bentinck called the consolidator of British Empire. True: Hastings laid the civil administration base, Cornwallis built on it; Clive reformed services; Dalhousie annexed by Doctrine of Lapse.

44-006.r: Founder of the British Empire in India → Lord (Robert) Clive; came to Madras as a Company clerk in 1744; won Plassey in 1757.

44-007.r: Banaras Rebellion (1781) → led by Raja Chet Singh; Governor-General Warren Hastings fled to Chunar Fort.

44-008.r: Asiatic Society, Calcutta, founded 15 January 1784 → Governor-General of Bengal then was Warren Hastings.

44-009.r: 'Security cell' / Ring Fence policy → Warren Hastings (also Wellesley): buffer states like Oudh protected at their own cost against Afghans and Marathas.

44-011.r: Dual Government in Bengal abolished → Warren Hastings (Court of Directors' decision, 1772); he dismissed deputy Diwans Muhammad Raza Khan and Raja Shitab Roy.

44-012.r: Dual Government in Bengal → started by Robert Clive in 1765; administration split into Diwani (revenue) and Nizamat.
44-012.h: Clive starts it, Warren Hastings ends it.

44-013.r: Governor-General impeached by British Parliament → Warren Hastings, tried 1788-1795 for arbitrary acts; all charges dropped.

44-015.r: Vellore Mutiny (1806) → under Governor-General Sir George Barlow; sepoys protested interference in social and religious customs and raised the Mysore ruler's flag.

44-016.r: Judicial organisation in India → Lord Cornwallis; Company took justice from the Nawab in 1790; he set up circuit courts under a superior court.

44-017.r: Covenanted Civil Service (later ICS) → Cornwallis; his "Cornwallis Code" separated civil (revenue) and judicial administration.

44-019.r: Daroga → local face of "Company Bahadur's" authority; Cornwallis (1793) took police duty from zamindars and put a Daroga, under the Magistrate, over each police station.

44-020.r: Tomb of Lord Cornwallis → Ghazipur (U.P.); he died there on 5 Oct 1805; Governor-General 1786-1793 and again 1805; known for Permanent Settlement.

44-021.r: Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance aimed at: big army at others' cost, safety from Napoleon, British paramountcy - not a fixed income for the Company.

44-022.r: First Maratha chief to accept Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance → Peshwa Bajirao II. Terms: British troops in his state at his cost, plus a British Resident.

44-023.r: Treaty of Bassein (Vasai), 31 Dec 1802 → English East India Company and Peshwa Bajirao II; about 6 thousand British troops at Pune, paid by 26 lakh.
44-023.t: Bajirao II, not Bajirao I; English, not French or Dutch.

44-024.r: First Indian ruler in a subsidiary-type alliance → Nawab of Oudh; Wellesley (1798-1805) only gave the old system its final shape; Dupleix first lent troops for payment.
44-024.t: Under Wellesley's formal system, the first to sign was the Nizam of Hyderabad.

44-026.r: Subsidiary Alliance order: Hyderabad (1798, 1800), Mysore and Tanjore (1799), Awadh (1801), Peshwa (1802), Bhonsle (1803), Scindia (1804); Holkar only 1818.
44-026.c: Answer not printed; explanation lists Hyderabad, Mysore, Holkar (1818) and Jodhpur as all accepting, so no option clearly fits.

44-029.r: Subsidiary Alliance System → Lord Wellesley, Governor-General 1798-1805; first to join → Nizam of Hyderabad.

44-030.r: Main aim of Subsidiary Alliance with Rajput states → to establish British sovereignty over Indian states.

44-031.r: Wrong pair: Subsidiary Alliance 1863 → actually 1798 (Wellesley; Hyderabad first). Correct: Buxar 1764; trade opened to British citizens 1813; Company monopoly 1833.

44-032.r: When Napoleon was crushing European empires, Lord Wellesley kept the British flag high in India, using the Subsidiary Alliance against the French threat.

44-033.r: Anglo-Nepal War (1814-16) → under Lord Hastings; ended by Treaty of Sugauli, signed 2 Dec 1815, ratified 4 March 1816.
44-033.t: Lord Hastings (Nepal war) is not Warren Hastings.

44-035.r: Treaty of Sugauli (1816): Nepal ceded Kumaon, eastern Garhwal and parts of Terai → Ranikhet and Nainital came to the British; Kathmandu stayed Nepal's capital.
